summary:
North Carolina is a state within the United States, and a trans visitor stands under the federal framework before any state rule applies. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas, and directed the attorney general to "correct the misapplication" of Bostock v. Clayton County (2020). The same order required federal agencies to use "sex" rather than "gender," mandated removal of materials promoting what the order calls gender ideology, and rescinded policies requiring use of names and pronouns consistent with a person's gender identity in federal workplaces. The facilities bar reaches federal buildings in North Carolina.

The State Department has stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents, and passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until expiry. The X marker had been available since 2022. In November 2025 the Supreme Court allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992, and the restriction remains challenged in federal courts. The ACLU sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and by March 2025 trans and nonbinary travellers reported passports being confiscated or blocked at processing, with some left stranded abroad.

Entry screening carries its own exposure. An executive order titled "Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports" was issued on 5 February 2025, and on 25 February 2025 the State Department announced it would bar trans athletes from entering the United States to compete in women's sports, flagging visa applicants with an internal marking and treating as fraud, with a permanent bar, any applicant listing a gender other than the one assigned at birth. The Transportation Security Administration's checkpoint procedures involve secondary screening, hand-held devices and pat-downs that can be invasive of privacy and risk outing a trans traveller.

Gender-affirming care is restricted on several fronts. Executive Order 14187 of 28 January 2025 described such care for minors as mutilation and some hospitals paused care; in summer 2025 the Department of Justice subpoenaed more than 20 hospitals for full records of patients under 19, including names, social security numbers and doctors' notes. Gender-affirming care for children is banned in 27 states, and in October 2025 proposed health-department rules would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18. In July 2025 the federal government shut down specialised LGBTQ youth services on the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline.

Custody is a documented site of harm. From 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted Florida-based policies for transgender inmates that mandate cutting their hair short, withdrawing hormone medication and substituting psychiatric therapy and psychiatric drugs; imprisoned transgender people reported being denied care, and the Bureau of Prisons stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners it holds from 2025. In immigration detention, transgender men were subjected to forced-labour programmes with guards justifying them by saying they would treat them "like a man," and those who refused faced beatings and solitary confinement; severe sexual abuse was also widely reported.

Official hostility extends to enforcement machinery. In December 2025 the attorney general instructed the FBI to offer cash bounties for information leading to the identification and arrest of transgender activists promoting what she called radical gender ideology, describing such activists as domestic terrorist groups. A May 2026 national counterterrorism strategy stated that counterterrorism activity would prioritise the rapid identification and neutralisation of groups whose ideology is described as anti-American, radically pro-transgender and anarchist.

Other federal measures in force or in litigation include the military purge under Executive Order 14183, the women's sports ban under Executive Order 14201, a January 2025 federal funding freeze, and an October 2025 rule blocking student loan forgiveness for public workers who provide gender-affirming care to transgender youth. Several of these orders have been blocked or enjoined in court, so the operative position on any given measure should be checked before travel.

At state level, facility rules are the defining North Carolina question. After the Charlotte city council passed an ordinance in March 2016 allowing transgender people to use bathrooms matching their gender identity, the North Carolina General Assembly met in emergency session and passed House Bill 2, which barred cities from passing anti-discrimination ordinances protecting gay and transgender people and required people to use public bathrooms corresponding with the sex listed on their birth certificate. The law drew global backlash, with companies including Google and Disney pledging to pull back business, and the U.S. Justice Department called it "state-sponsored discrimination" and sued, while North Carolina filed its own suit. Legislators repealed House Bill 2 on 30 March 2017 in the face of the boycotts.

Facility use remains an active legislative subject in North Carolina. In the 2025 session Republican lawmakers were again pushing a transgender bathroom bill, years after the HB 2 boycotts forced the repeal, so a visitor should expect facilities access to be contested rather than settled.

Lethal violence against trans people in North Carolina does not track the state's protective posture. A July 2026 investigative data analysis comparing legal-risk tiers with Trans Murder Monitoring records found that protective statutes do not predict lower lethal risk for trans women; its state rate chart places North Carolina at 3.0 killings per 100,000 trans women, on a recorded base of three or more victims that the analysis acknowledges is an undercount, and characterises the state as moderate-risk. That rating describes recorded killings and should not be read as an assurance of safety for an individual visitor.
tangentialFactors:
Nationwide, state bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and, in some states, government buildings cover 9 states and 1 territory, with some states making trans use of facilities a criminal offence in certain circumstances; 29 states, 4 territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban. North Carolina's 2016-2017 episode sits on the protective side of that split in its outcome, yet the 2025 bill push shows the position is unstable.

Enforcement of facility laws elsewhere has produced arrests. In April 2025 a trans student was arrested and handcuffed in a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol after declaring an intention to break the law; civil-rights attorneys described it as the first known arrest under a state bathroom-restriction law. That incident indicates how a restored North Carolina rule could be enforced against someone who tests it deliberately or by mistake.

Identity documents are being closed in other state legislatures in ways that travel to North Carolina. In March 2026 Kansas enacted a law invalidating birth certificates and driver's licences that do not match sex assigned at birth and barring trans people from sex-segregated facilities, which rights groups call a template for other state legislatures, with further targeting bills pending. Equality-map research shows the conditions for changing a gender marker on a licence or birth certificate differ state by state.

The North Carolina data point in the July 2026 violence analysis is drawn from a national chart whose author flags the murder counts as an undercount, so the 3.0 per 100,000 figure should be treated as a floor rather than a measurement.
localsOnly:
North Carolina residents live under the federal facilities bar wherever federal buildings are involved, and the HB 2 repeal removed the state's birth-certificate-sex bathroom mandate in 2017, leaving facility rules to whatever the General Assembly passes next.

Local governments in North Carolina are barred by the HB 2 framework from passing their own anti-discrimination ordinances protecting gay and transgender people, so municipal protections are not a reliable substitute for state law. Charlotte's March 2016 ordinance was the trigger for that preemption.

Residents who wish to change a gender marker on a North Carolina licence or birth certificate face state-specific requirements that the sources consulted here do not set out. Marker-change conditions for trans residents are not established in this record.

Facility-use policy is an open legislative matter in the current session, and residents bear the consequences of any restored mandate directly, including in schools, government buildings and public accommodations.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 2025 North Carolina bathroom bill was enacted is unresolved in the sources consulted; it is described as being pushed in the session, not as having passed.

The current status of each federal executive order is unresolved here. Several have been blocked or enjoined in court, and the record does not establish which provisions were operative on a given date.

North Carolina's own hate-crime statute, its treatment of gender-affirming care for minors, and its marriage or partner-recognition position are not sourced in the material reviewed and are therefore not asserted.

The conditions for changing a gender marker on a North Carolina driver's licence or birth certificate are not established in the sources consulted, although equality-map research indicates these differ state by state.

The 3.0 per 100,000 trans-women killing rate for North Carolina comes from an analysis that states its own victim counts are undercounts; no independent confirmation of the underlying records appears in this material.
